newsitem.title: JAPAN: Energy saving by developing nations crucial - report.
newsitem.headline: Energy saving by developing nations crucial - report.

text.p: Industrialised nations' efforts to curb carbon dioxide emissions and conserve energy are not expected to be effective without cooperation from developing countries, a report by Japan's Institute of Energy Economics (IEE) said.

"Developed countries are setting targets for the amount of carbon dioxide emissions they aim to cut. However, such efforts may lose their meaning unless they are combined with efforts by developing countries," Toshiaki Yuasa, an IEE economist, told reporters on Wednesday.
In 1995, industrialised countries signed a United Nations convention committing them to cut emissions from burning fossil fuel, blamed as the cause of global warming, back to 1990 levels by 2000.

In a study on the outlook for the energy supply-and-demand situation until 2100, global energy demand that year is forecast to be the equivalent of about 34 billion tonnes of oil -- about seven times more than current levels, Yuasa said. The outlook takes into account restrictions on energy resources and the environment,

"If developing countries improve their energy efficiency to Japan's standards, global energy demand in 2100 can be lowered by about 12 percent to 30 billion tonnes oil-equivalent," he said. Japan's energy efficiency is high, even compared to that of other developed nations, he added.
Global carbon dioxide emissions in 2100 are estimated at 40 billion tonnes carbon-equivalent, but could be cut back considerably if developing countries reduce their energy consumption, Yuasa said.
"It is estimated that efforts by developing countries to save energy could reduce the 2100 total by about 12 billion tonnes carbon-equivalent," he said.
According to the IEE, proven recoverable reserves of crude oil will run dry between 2020 and 2030, natural gas in 2040 and coal between 2050 and 2060.
"After proved recoverable reserves have been consumed, we will have to rely on costlier, undiscovered energy resources," Yuasa said.
